item.title: Property Finder uncovers label bias and improves vision AI with Amazon Bedrock
item.description:
Property Finder uncovers label bias and improves vision AI with Amazon Bedrock

Property Finder’s engineering team discovered that 96.8 percent of their image‑evaluation labels were inherited directly from a single vision‑language model instead of being verified by human experts. By building an unbiased ground‑truth set and applying evolutionary prompt optimization on Amazon Bedrock, they achieved higher accuracy while cutting costs by 86 percent.

🔍 Overview

  • Co‑authored with Khaled Thabit, Meriem Boughrara, and Mohamed Desouky from Property Finder.
  • The issue was uncovered while migrating the vision AI workload to a more cost‑effective option on Amazon Bedrock.
  • Property Finder processes tens of thousands of property images each day across the MENA region, with thousands of new listings averaging 15 images that must be quality‑checked before going live.

🏗️ Evaluation Bias Discovery

  • 96.8 % of the existing evaluation labels came from the predictions of a single VLM, never independently verified.
  • This left any alternative model structurally disadvantaged before any image was processed.
  • Specific problems identified:
    • Watermark text extraction showed character‑level mistakes marked as correct, including hallucinated brand names and missing characters.
    • Photo classification forced a single label onto images that contained multiple room types.
    • In the remaining 3.2 % of human‑labeled samples, annotators introduced categories outside the original specification (e.g., “Office” where no such label existed in the prompt).

🛠️ Building Unbiased Ground Truth

  • The team hand‑annotated 356 UAE images and a separate set of Egypt images, selected from unlabeled production listings across representative industry segments.
  • The first 256 UAE images formed the development set for prompt tuning.
  • An evaluation set uses all 356 images plus 100 newly annotated images to compare the final model.
  • A strategy and analytics expert annotated all images; the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team performed systematic quality reviews to resolve ambiguous cases and keep labeling consistent.
  • A set of 356 images is considered roughly sufficient to detect moderate differences between models.

🤖 Prompt Optimization on Amazon Bedrock

  • Property Finder processed each image with Amazon Bedrock, which returns predicted attributes in JSON format.
  • During optimization, predictions were scored with Micro F1 against the 256‑image expert‑annotated development set.
  • The optimization loop ran from v0 to v27:
    • Early versions used AI assistants to refine prompts.
    • Later versions employed automated optimization.
  • Switching from single‑label to multi‑label classification removed a major source of artificial ambiguity and allowed measurement of correct secondary predictions.

📊 Results

  • The selected model on Amazon Bedrock delivered higher accuracy while reducing inference cost by 86 percent compared with the legacy approach.
  • The unbiased ground‑truth data eliminated the structural disadvantage previously faced by alternative models.

💡 Why it Matters

  • Property Finder evaluates 11 quality attributes per image, covering:
    • Watermark detection
    • Room classification
    • Furnishing status
    • Photo quality
    • Construction indicators
  • Reliable quality assessment is essential for tens of thousands of daily listings before they appear to users.
  • A hybrid approach—combining models from different families, surfacing candidate labels and disagreements, and having human experts adjudicate—ensures no model output is used directly as a label.

Attribute Coverage (sample)

Attribute Category Example
Watermark detection Detects embedded branding or text watermarks
Room classification Identifies living room, kitchen, bedroom, etc.
Furnishing status Determines whether a room is furnished
Photo quality Assesses resolution, lighting, and composition
Construction indicators Flags signs of construction or renovation

#PropertyFinder #ComputerVision #AmazonBedrock #DataQuality

Source: Fix evaluation bias to unlock better models on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS adds continuous quality loop to Bedrock AgentCore multi‑agent sales system
item.description:
AWS adds continuous quality loop to Bedrock AgentCore multi‑agent sales system

AWS SMGS Operations team updated its production multi‑agent solution with a continuous quality loop built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The loop monitors answer correctness and traces failures back to data, prompts, or code.

🔍 Overview

  • The system lets sellers and sales leaders ask business questions in plain English from Amazon Quick.
  • Answers are scoped to the user’s territory and role‑level security.
  • Field teams rely on the answers for account‑strategy planning and customer‑meeting preparation.

🧩 How it works

  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore orchestrates several specialized sub‑agents that each own a distinct capability domain.
  • Upstream pipelines refresh the underlying data every week.
  • Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, CloudWatch, S3, Redshift, Quick, and Lambda provide safety, observability, and persistence.

⚙️ Continuous quality loop

  • Monitoring stays green across runs, but the system only reports that it responded, not whether the answer is correct.
  • Errors observed in pre‑production include:
    • Reporting a $410.08 M revenue figure when the source was $410.08.
    • Labeling Sales Revenue as “Sales Revenue excluding Adjustments.”
    • Offering an Annual Recurring Revenue estimate that does not exist in the data.
    • Presenting its own calculations as sourced facts.
  • Risk grows with each new agent and any change to data, prompts, code, or models.
  • Coordinated releases can create a mismatch window where a data change, tool change, and prompt update land separately; a pre‑production test showed this dropped the pass rate from 78 % to 38 %.
  • To address these risks, a framework is required that:
    • Shows whether answers are grounded and correct before every release and continuously in production.
    • Traces each failure back to its root cause—data, prompt, or agent code.

📊 Impact

  • Serves two audiences:
    1. Field sales teams – replaces hours of manual analysis with on‑demand conversational intelligence, surfacing risks and opportunities.
    2. Leadership – powers Weekly Business Reviews and other cadences without manual report preparation.
  • The same agentic system is used both on the front line and at scale for performance review.

🗂️ Components

Sub‑Agent Capability
Performance Insights Agent Generates natural‑language business‑intelligence narratives from complex sales data, scoped to territory.
Customer Insights Agent Synthesizes product usage, support history, contract status, and engagement data into a 360° customer view.
Data Insights Agent Provides text‑to‑SQL querying of structured analytics data in plain English.
Direct Dashboard Access Allows users to view underlying dashboards directly from the conversational interface.

🛠️ Underlying services

  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – core orchestration and evaluation (AgentCore Evaluations).
  • Amazon Bedrock Guardrails – safety layer.
  • Amazon CloudWatch – metrics, alarms, tracing.
  • Amazon S3 & Amazon Redshift – evaluation persistence.
  • Amazon Quick – dashboard rendering.
  • AWS Lambda – custom evaluators.

#AWS #Bedrock #AIAgents #DataQuality

Source: Building trust in AI agents: A production-ready evaluation framework with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services

item.title: 🔍 Shadows in Plain Sight: How RAG Systems Can Silently Distort Your LLM's Output
item.description:
🔍 Shadows in Plain Sight: How RAG Systems Can Silently Distort Your LLM’s Output

Summary: This eye-opening technical exploration reveals how Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems can introduce subtle but dangerous distortions in LLM outputs. We examine real-world examples, identify key risk factors, and offer practical strategies for detecting and mitigating these “shadow distortions” to build more reliable AI systems.

🌟 The Invisible Problem with RAG Systems

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful approach for enhancing Large Language Models (LLMs) with external knowledge. By retrieving relevant information from a knowledge base and incorporating it into the generation process, RAG systems help ground LLMs in factual information, reducing hallucinations and improving accuracy.

But what happens when the retrieval mechanism introduces its own subtle distortions?

I recently observed something concerning while working with several RAG implementations: the retrieved context can silently bias or distort the LLM’s output in ways that are difficult to detect but potentially harmful. I call these “shadow distortions” - subtle shifts in reasoning, framing, or conclusions that occur when an LLM processes imperfectly retrieved information.

🔬 Understanding Shadow Distortions

Shadow distortions occur when the retrieval component of a RAG system returns information that is:

  1. 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁 but contextually misaligned
  2. Factually correct but 𝙞𝙣𝙘𝙤𝙢𝙥𝙡𝙚𝙩𝙚 in critical ways
  3. Subtly biased in perspective or framing

Here’s a real-world example I encountered: When asking a RAG system about climate change mitigation strategies, the retrieval component returned technically relevant documents about carbon capture technology. However, 90% of the retrieved information focused on a single, controversial approach while omitting mainstream alternatives. The LLM’s response then overemphasized this approach, creating a distorted picture of expert consensus.

📸 See illustration below showing how different retrieval results on the same topic can lead to dramatically different LLM outputs despite using identical prompts and model parameters.

What makes these distortions particularly dangerous is that they’re often imperceptible to end users. The output appears authoritative and well-reasoned, with no obvious hallucinations or factual errors. But the underlying reasoning and context have been subtly warped.

🧪 The Anatomy of Distortion

Through extensive testing, I’ve identified four primary mechanisms through which shadow distortions manifest:

1. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗧𝘂𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴

When the retrieval system returns documents focused on a narrow subset of perspectives, the LLM can produce responses that mirror this tunnel vision. Even if the LLM has broader knowledge in its parameters, the immediate context often dominates its reasoning process.

1
2
3

Example: Query about cryptocurrency regulation →
Retrieved documents all discussing one country's approach →
Response presents that country's approach as universal

2. 𝑆𝑒𝑚𝑎𝑛𝑡𝑖𝑐 𝐵𝑙𝑒𝑒𝑑𝑖𝑛𝑔

The emotional tone, terminology preference, or rhetorical style of retrieved documents can “bleed” into the LLM’s response, even when the factual content remains accurate. This subtly shifts the framing without changing the core facts.

1
2
3

Example: Medical query →
Retrieved documents using alarmist language →
Response maintains technical accuracy but adopts anxiety-inducing framing

3. 🔄 Reference Amplification

When multiple retrieved documents reference the same source or perspective, the LLM tends to overweight its importance, creating an artificial consensus effect.

4. 𝙏𝙚𝙢𝙥𝙤𝙧𝙖𝙡 𝙎𝙠𝙚𝙬𝙞𝙣𝙜

Retrieval systems that over-index on either very recent or older documents can create misleading temporal context, making outdated information seem current or new developments seem established.

🛡️ Detecting and Mitigating Shadow Distortions

After identifying these patterns, I developed several techniques to detect and mitigate shadow distortions:

Detection Strategies:

  1. Perspective Contrast Testing: Run the same query through multiple knowledge bases with known different perspectives and compare outputs.

  2. Semantic Diversity Analysis: Quantitatively measure the diversity of viewpoints, sources, and temporal distribution in retrieved documents.

  3. 🔍 Explanation Chain Analysis: Require the LLM to explain its reasoning process and reference sources, then check for over-reliance on particular retrieved documents.

Mitigation Approaches:

  1. Explicit Diversity Enforcement: Modify retrieval algorithms to ensure representation of multiple perspectives, time periods, and source types.

  2. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗕𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗴: Include explicit instructions for the LLM to consider the limitations of the provided context.

  3. Metadata Awareness: Add metadata to retrieved documents indicating their recency, perspective alignment, and coverage completeness.

  4. Multi-stage Retrieval: Implement a two-pass system where initial retrieval results are analyzed for diversity before final context selection.

📸 See diagram below showing a multi-stage retrieval system with diversity checks built in.

🧠 Building More Robust RAG Systems

The reality is that no retrieval system will be perfect. The key to building robust RAG systems lies in acknowledging these limitations and designing systems that compensate for them.

A promising approach is what I call “𝘾𝙤𝙣𝙩𝙚𝙭𝙩-𝘼𝙬𝙖𝙧𝙚 𝙍𝘼𝙂” - systems that explicitly model the strengths and limitations of their retrieval components and adjust accordingly. This involves:

  1. Explicitly communicating retrieval confidence and coverage to the LLM
  2. Training LLMs to reason about the completeness of retrieved information
  3. Implementing circuit breakers that flag potential shadow distortions to users

The most effective approach combines technical improvements with transparency. When a system might be operating with incomplete information, it should communicate this limitation rather than producing a confident but potentially distorted response.

💭 The Path Forward

Shadow distortions represent a subtle but significant challenge for RAG systems. As these systems become more widely deployed in critical applications like healthcare, education, and information retrieval, addressing these distortions becomes increasingly important.

The good news is that being aware of the problem is half the solution. By implementing the detection and mitigation strategies outlined above, we can build RAG systems that leverage the power of external knowledge while minimizing the risk of invisible distortions.

As we move forward, I believe we need to shift our evaluation metrics for RAG systems beyond simple retrieval precision and recall to include measures of perspective diversity, temporal balance, and distortion resistance.

What invisible distortions might be lurking in your RAG systems right now, and how will you bring them into the light?
